cards.explanation: The answer is once all the flocks are gathered there. That's the well's rule. When all the flocks have been gathered, the shepherds roll the stone away, water the sheep, and put the stone back over the mouth of the well (Genesis 29:3). It's like waiting for the whole batch to cool before anybody touches a cookie. Nobody gets a head start.

The answer is Haran. Jacob asks, “where are you from?” and the shepherds answer, “We are from Haran…” (Genesis 29:4) That's the very place Jacob was headed when he left Beersheba (Genesis 28:10). He asked a stranger one simple question and landed right on target.

The answer is False. The shepherds know Laban. Jacob asks about Laban the grandson of Nahor, and they say, “We know him…” (Genesis 29:5). Then they tell Jacob Laban is well. I bet Jacob was smiling by then.

The answer is Rachel. She is Laban's daughter, and the shepherds say she's coming with his sheep (Genesis 29:6). She is also a shepherdess, so those sheep are hers to look after (Genesis 29:9). Keep that name in your pocket, friends.

The answer is to water the sheep and take them back to pasture. It's still broad daylight, so Jacob tells the shepherds to do just that (Genesis 29:7). Brand new in town and already giving orders at the well. Confidence, friends.

The answer is True. As soon as Jacob sees Rachel with Laban's sheep, he goes up, rolls the stone away from the mouth of the well, and waters his uncle's sheep (Genesis 29:10). Just before this, the shepherds told him, “We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered and the stone has been rolled away…” (Genesis 29:8). Then Jacob walks up and rolls it himself, like that stone owed him money!

The answer is that she runs and tells her father. Jacob tells Rachel he's Rebekah's son and a relative of her father, and she ran and told her father (Genesis 29:12). She didn't walk. Good news travels fast, friends.

The answer is False. Laban doesn't wait at home. When he heard the news about his sister's son Jacob, he ran out to meet him (Genesis 29:13). He embraced him, kissed him, and brought him home. Nobody had to knock on his door.

The answer is True. After Jacob has told him all that had happened, Laban declares, “You are indeed my own flesh and blood.” (Genesis 29:14) Jacob is Laban's sister's son, so it fits. I think that was a warm welcome for a traveler who'd come a long way.

The answer is wages. Laban says, “Tell me what your wages should be.” (Genesis 29:15) He doesn't want his relative working for nothing. So Jacob gets to name his own price. That's a generous opening offer.

The answer is False. Rachel is the younger one. Laban's older daughter is Leah, and the younger is Rachel (Genesis 29:16). Leah first, Rachel second. Write it on your oven mitt, friends, because that order is about to matter.

The answer is seven. Jacob says, “I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel.” (Genesis 29:18) The text tells us he offers it because he loves her. Seven years is a long time to sign up for. That tells you where his heart is.

The answer is that it's better than giving her to another. Laban says, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” (Genesis 29:19) Notice he doesn't haggle or ask for more. He just says yes and tells Jacob to stay. Fastest deal in the whole passage, and the shortest seven-year contract negotiation ever!

The answer is like only a few days. The text says Jacob served seven years for Rachel, yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her (Genesis 29:20). Love changed how the time felt. Seven years like a few days is not how a Monday morning feels, friends.

The answer is False. When evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob (Genesis 29:23). Jacob had served seven years for Rachel, and the evening ended with Leah. This is a big turn in the story.
The answer is deceived. Jacob asks Laban, “Wasn’t it for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?” (Genesis 29:25) He had served seven years for Rachel. I think that morning hit him hard.

The answer is marrying off the younger daughter before the older. Laban says, “It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older.” (Genesis 29:26) Leah is the older daughter and Rachel is the younger (Genesis 29:16). That's the reason he gives Jacob.

The answer is another seven years of work. Laban says to finish the week's celebration, and they will give Jacob the younger one in return for another seven years of work (Genesis 29:27). That's seven more on top of the seven he's already put in. A long road for Jacob.

The answer is False. Jacob stays. He finishes the week's celebration, and Laban gives him Rachel as his wife (Genesis 29:28). Then the text says he worked for Laban another seven years (Genesis 29:30). Nobody packs a bag in this passage, friends, and seven more years is a LONG time to wait, so I think that tells you how much he loved her.

The answer is True. The text says it plainly: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah (Genesis 29:30). That's how it is in this house. I think this is a tender spot, and Leah's part of the story isn't finished.
